title: How Justin Rose and McLaren are pursuing marginal gains in golf
excerpt:
At the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, Justin Rose reflected on his first months as McLaren Golf's inaugural ambassador, his year spent testing prototype irons with the McLaren engineering team, and a partnership he hopes will bring Formula 1's obsession with marginal gains to his pursuit of a second major.

Cast an eye to the fringes of the tree-lined fairways at Wentworth Club, the home of this week’s BMW PGA Championship, and you may spot more papaya-clad spectators than you might expect at a golf event.

But since McLaren entered the world of golf in stunning fashion ahead of this year’s Miami Grand Prix, unveiling its first set of clubs and announcing its partnership with Justin Rose, the grandstands around the greens of the PGA and DP World Tours are starting to look a little brighter – not least at the historic venue to the west of London where the concept of the Ryder Cup was first proposed in 1926.

Wentworth is a mere 15-minute drive from the McLaren Technology Centre, and with Rose also based locally, it is as much a ‘home’ tournament for the player as it is for his new clubs.

Back in April, the launch of McLaren Golf, with Rose as their first global ambassador and investor, turned heads just as intended on both the grid and the greens. The 46-year-old immediately switched out his clubs for the PGA Tour’s Cadillac Championship, also in Miami that week.

'Scrapping for the finest of margins'

“I’m loving it,” says Rose, the 2013 US Open champion and Rio 2016 Olympic gold medallist. Even as one of a handful of players on tour over the age of 40, he continues to contend at the majors: runner-up finishes at The Open in 2024 and the Masters in 2025 were followed by a tie for third at Augusta in 2026.

No doubt part of Rose’s calculation in linking up with McLaren is the hope of converting those near-misses into victories.

“The culture around F1 is all about scrapping for the finest of margins when every millisecond counts,” Rose continues. “Hopefully that’s a good ethos to bring into the golf world as well.”

He admits, “My brother’s the petrolhead of our family,” before adding, “I could claim myself to be a Drive to Survive bandwagon fan, but I was very aware of F1 growing up.

"We’ve been spoilt in the UK – it’s always been a sport we’ve been successful at, with great drivers through the years; Lewis [Hamilton], of course, and so many before him.

“But in recent years, living so close to Woking and the MTC, and being asked to be involved on the McLaren advisory board, has given me much greater appreciation of the sport. And it’s been nice getting to know Zak [Brown], Lando [Norris] and the boys. When you know people personally, you start to pay more attention.”

Irons in the fire

Naturally, McLaren’s fans have embraced Rose as one of their own with the 46-year-old joining McLaren CEO Brown for Wednesday’s pro-am event; Norris, an avid golfer, was also slated to play, only for a sore back to leave him watching from the sidelines.

But even with his F1 stablemates elsewhere as the first round began on Thursday, McLaren caps and polos were a regular feature among the spectators huddled near the tee boxes and greens.

While Rose’s papaya McLaren bag has certainly caught the eye since April, his new clubs have sparked the most discussion. The former World No.1 was instrumental in the development and testing of the prototype range of irons, working with McLaren’s engineers for over a year before debuting the clubs on the professional stage.

What really excites him is what comes next: helping to develop McLaren Golf’s first drivers and woods, where applying the full weight of McLaren’s world-class research, design, and engineering expertise will truly unlock the project’s full potential.

“The irons project, which is the first venture, is a little bit more straightforward, [but that’s] not to say that we’re not doing anything differently,” explains Rose.

“It’s cool that McLaren have come to market with metal-injection moulded irons. It is not necessarily a new process, but it’s a new way for someone to build the clubs start to finish.

“Once we get into the metal woods, the fairway woods, and the drivers, that’s when the wind tunnel, the algorithmic building, CADs and aerodynamic science will be very valuable to us.”

Shared sporting DNA

At first glance, Formula 1 and golf may appear to live at opposing ends of the sporting spectrum; Oscar Piastri’s mother Nicole once said she wished her son had pursued a career in either golf or tennis for the sake of her nerves, but could not stand in the way of his F1 dreams.

But there are parallels, not least in the mentality, concentration, problem-solving and precision under pressure required from its protagonists. But while Norris is an ardent golfer in his spare time, ask Rose if he would ever want to trade places with him or Piastri, and his response suggests he won’t be swapping fairways for the pit lane any time soon.

“It’s phenomenal what they do,” Rose says. “I think we all think we’re okay behind the wheel, but then you get an understanding of where your limits are in a car, and it’s not where their limits are. It’s scary, actually, to see what they can do in a machine like that.

“My only experience is being taken on a hot lap in a McLaren, not even an F1 car. To see what those boys are capable of is quite frightening and awe-inspiring. But keep that on the track!”

title: Inside F1’s ‘brutal’ fuel development race
excerpt:
Not only did F1 introduce new cars and new power units at the start of the 2026 season, but also Advanced Sustainable Fuels, a pioneering technology that teams – and their partners – have been pushing hard to maximise in terms of both performance and reliability.

The story behind F1’s new fuels

Prior to this year’s rules reset, F1 already boasted the most efficient engines on the planet with turbo-hybrid power units that used 10% ethanol biofuel – a small part of the sport’s commitment to becoming Net Zero by 2030.

However, that was stepped up a gear for 2026, with F1 and its governing body, the FIA, mandating Advanced Sustainable Fuels made from sources such as carbon capture (taking CO2 directly from the air or industrial emissions), municipal waste and non-food biomass.

Sometimes described as ‘drop-in’ fuels, they are designed to replace fossil fuel equivalents without any adjustments being required inside the engine, meaning that, in theory, they can be used in road cars.

Over the last couple of years, in the build-up to F1’s new era, F1 squads and their fuel partners cycled through a host of product iterations to find the perfect blend and hit the ground running at the Barcelona Shakedown in January.

For Audi, that meant working closely with technology partner BP, who assessed 70 fuel components and developed 400 pilot fuel samples before the 2026 campaign, while testing 200 fuel blends in the German manufacturer’s all-new power unit and delivering 240,000 litres of test fuel to their Neuburg facility.

“There are two things here,” says Luc Jolly, BP’s Motorsports Technology Fluid Lead, in conversation with F1.com. “One is that Audi are a new team, with a brand-new power unit, working to a new regulation set, and secondly, there’s the Advanced Sustainable Fuels requirement.

“We know the types of fuel components, molecules, additives and things that have typically worked well in F1 engines in the past, but essentially, all of the fossil-based componentry that we’d normally use, and was very well established, was not available to us.

“We’ve had to kind of start from scratch in terms of what works really well in the Audi engine, while that’s been developing, and then once we know what works, how do we do that in an advanced, sustainable way, that the FIA will approve?”

Performance vs reliability

As touched on in our introduction, finding the perfect balance between performance and reliability is easier said than done, especially at the start of a new ruleset – but Jolly and his dedicated BP motorsport team embraced that task from the outset.

“For people like me, it’s an awesome technical challenge,” adds Jolly. “That is why we like F1. Yes, it’s about the drivers, the fans, the passion, and all those kinds of things, but it’s also a technical sport. If you didn’t get these new things coming along that shake things up a bit, it wouldn’t be F1, would it?

“F1 is the pinnacle of motorsport and engineering, and with anything in engineering there’s that trade-off between performance, how well something’s going to perform, and how much margin we have to leave in terms of reliability.

“Obviously we have the regulations in F1 around how many engines you can use per year, and the ideal scenario is that you don’t over-engineer. That’s a major consideration. We’re trying to find the sweet spot of being just reliable enough, so you unlock the maximum performance, and that’s not something you necessarily absolutely nail in year one.

“The competition in F1 is absolutely brutal. Everyone’s got talented people, right? But we’re on that journey, and it’s about who develops the quickest, and we think this year we’re building really strong foundations.”

Also present for our fuel deep-dive is Gabriel Bortoleto, who made his F1 debut with Sauber in 2025 before the team transitioned to Audi’s works effort – the Brazilian sharing his own fascination about what has gone into F1’s 2026 fuels.

“We were downstairs just before you guys came in and had a chat,” says Bortoleto, pointing in Jolly’s direction. “I was asking him all my questions, and I had so many more questions that I would [end up asking him] for the rest of the day!

“It’s funny, because I grew up literally driving, driving, driving, driving, and you keep driving and evolving your techniques on the driving side, but when you reach F1, it’s a completely different world. It’s all about innovation, it’s all about bringing upgrades to the car, to the engine, in the fuel, in every component in the car.

“I feel like my life has changed in the last year in that sense. I was used to driving with one chassis, with one fuel supplier, with one engine supplier all my life, and now it's a different topic. With BP and Audi, it has been completely different, and it’s been very interesting so far to learn about many of these topics.

“My part and my involvement can only be once I jump in the car on the track, and I give feedback. I don’t go to the lab and tell the guys, ‘Look, I need more!’ I just give the feedback of what I feel about the engine, and then that passes through the areas it needs to go.”

Jolly jumps back in: “It’s an important part of it. We’re continually looking for the next upgrade, the next optimisations. Now that we’re racing, there is information coming back from the engineers at the track, which will have come from the drivers. Even though me and Gabi aren’t talking every day, it’s part of the whole picture.”

The future of Advanced Sustainable Fuels

So, with those next upgrades and optimisations in mind, how much more scope for development does Jolly see when it comes to Advanced Sustainable Fuels over the next few years?

“There’s always scope for continuing to develop,” Jolly makes clear. “In the first year of a new regulation cycle, and you’ll see it with all the teams, it’s that race of bringing upgrades, bringing more performance.

“I don’t think anyone would be in a position this year where they’re thinking there’s no more performance to be had – there’s plenty more.

“The other key thing to mention is with the regulations being adjusted [for 2027], and the increased fuel flow to rebalance the combustion power versus the electrical power, that is going to bring opportunities, and that will change fundamentally how the fuel performs in the engine.

“It’s a lot more complicated than just putting more fuel in. It really alters the dynamics inside the engine. So, I think even if it wasn’t for that, there would be more to do, but now there’s kind of change on change being added.”

While F1 remains the focus for Jolly’s engineers, there is potential – as touched on above – for Advanced Sustainable Fuels to be used in road cars moving forward.

There have also been on-track demonstrations from Sebastian Vettel and his ‘Race Without Trace’ project in recent times, with sustainable fuels powering a Nigel Mansell Williams FW14B, an Ayrton Senna McLaren MP4/8, and his own Red Bull RB9.

“In terms of some of the componentry, the additive chemistry, and how you make the combustion work better, the processes… those are the types of things we’re learning,” explains Jolly, when it comes to F1’s latest fuel technology making its way into road cars.

“At the moment, my team and I are fully focused on giving Audi the best performance possible, but we are part of the same team that’s developing BP Ultimate road fuels. We’re very well connected, we’re sharing learnings. As we’re going through this, we’re considering what from the stuff that we’re doing in the F1-dedicated team could potentially be of benefit to road fuel customers.

“Again, it’s about the journey, and we’re on that journey. The development cycle for F1 has to be very quick, and commercial stuff tends to take a bit longer. So, it’s a little bit down the road, but we’re on the learning journey with them.”

title: How 46 fashion designers reimagined McLaren’s F1 history
excerpt:
On Wednesday evening, the McLaren Technology Centre looked markedly different having been transformed into a fashion runway.

Instead of team personnel, it was models walking between some of McLaren's most famous cars that took centre stage, wearing a very different interpretation of the team’s history.

This was Designed to Race: Front Row, a show where 46 MA fashion students from Central Saint Martins presented 12 looks inspired by more than six decades of McLaren history.

James Hunt’s approach to racewear was one of the clearest references in the collection. So was the yellow of Ayrton Senna’s helmet, old racing equipment, engineering drawings and, much later in the collection, the papaya-clad fan culture surrounding the team today.

However, unlike many fashion collaborations, the students were not designing something for McLaren to sell.

“I think this was really about opening up a conversation,” McLaren Racing Chief Marketing Officer Louise McEwen exclusively told F1.com after the show. “The more we worked together, the more we realised, although we are in different spheres and different businesses, how similar we were.

“Both are incredible high-performing teams coming together with incredible craft, creativity and ingenuity at the heart of everything that we do. So it’s been a brilliant journey with them over the last nine months or so, coming up with the collections and working with the team there.”

The students had been split into 12 groups and handed a wide brief. A driver or famous car could be the starting point, but so could a period in McLaren’s history, the engineering behind the team or the people around it.

The finished collection moved through five chapters: Grit x Glamour, Precision and Power, Global Icon, Engineered Athlete and Papaya Era.

From the 1970s to Senna

The collection begins with the 1970s, when McLaren were establishing themselves as one of Formula 1’s leading teams.

Emerson Fittipaldi delivered McLaren’s first Drivers’ Championship in 1974, the same year they won their first Constructors’ Championship. Away from the results, F1 was changing too. Television audiences were growing and drivers were becoming increasingly recognisable away from the track.

James Hunt arrived at McLaren shortly afterwards and his unique style gave the students plenty to work with.

His habit of wearing his overalls tied around his waist, his disregard for formal dress and his wider image fed into Grit x Glamour. Flared silhouettes, leather, orange tones and distressed finishes all appeared, taking elements of Hunt’s style without simply recreating his wardrobe.

Speaking during a panel discussion ahead of the show, Central Saint Martins MA Fashion Course Leader Fabio Piras explained that the brief deliberately left room for that kind of interpretation.

“The brief was interesting because it wasn’t asking us to necessarily design a piece of fashion, an outfit," he said. "It was an interpretation of a period, of an era, of a character, of obviously an iconic champion and a car.

“I think the visit of the students to the Technology Centre was an absolutely bombastic moment for them, because actually you don’t realise how fantastic those cars are if you don’t see them closely, even in terms of design objects. They’re amazing design objects.”

For MA Fashion student Enzo Keuning, that freedom was what made the project interesting.

“What made this project unique was that there wasn’t one way to interpret that heritage. Each group brought a different perspective, from engineering and performance, to identity and craftsmanship, and we were challenged to transform those ideas into something new.

“My background in econometrics has taught me to look at systems through patterns, relationships and connections, so I found it fascinating to approach McLaren’s history through fashion.”

As the collection moved through McLaren’s history, some of the references became more technical. Senna’s famous yellow helmet was one of the clearest, but the students also looked at his precise driving style and the idea of speed. The resulting pieces used lightweight fabrics, shapes informed by airflow and digitally developed patterns.

Other groups looked away from the driver completely. One design centred on a female fire marshal, while track layouts, old team graphics and pieces of racing equipment appeared in smaller details throughout the collection.

Sometimes you had to look twice. Monaco’s famous hairpin, for example, was stitched inside a pair of trousers.

The details behind the clothes

Getting those 12 looks to the runway took months.

Fashion, Piras told the panel, is usually seen at the point where the work is already done. The audience gets the runway, but not the months of changing ideas, criticism and mistakes that came before it.

“When we see fashion, we always see the outcome. We see the 10-minute performance at the end. That’s the length of a fashion show.

“What an audience doesn’t have access to is the time it takes to get to those 10 outfits, in this case 12. The process of fashion is trial and error.

"You build the narrative, you build the information that will inform your fashion, but then it’s about trying things out and moving on with the mistakes. That’s how you create fashion.”

Piras’ description of trial and error was familiar territory for McLaren too, even if the measurements involved look very different.

During the panel, McEwen recalled how small the margins can become, using a request to save weight ahead of the 2025 British Grand Prix as an example.

“As a team, we’re in a constant state, similarly to Central Saint Martins, of reinvention. We have a saying that we absolutely can’t stand still because we have to keep innovating to stay at the front of the grid. If we don’t, we’re definitely going backwards.

“Even at the front, it boils down to microns and milliseconds that can make the difference between those grid positions for us.

“Last year, going into the British Grand Prix, our Team Principal said, ‘Lou, we need to save weight,’ and I can’t tell you how much, but it’s fair to say it was some segments of papaya that really make the difference. That’s the precision and detailing, and I think it was really evident working through the design process how much of that came through in the students’ designs.”

Engineering blueprints and aerodynamic forms fed into patterns and silhouettes, while carbon fibre and upcycled racing seatbelts were brought into the collection itself, with fabric offcuts, second-hand materials and used McLaren equipment also appearing across the 12 looks.

The Papaya era

Jump forward five decades and the references become perhaps easier to recognise.

Papaya dominates, racewear is mixed with denim and knitwear, and even Daniel Ricciardo’s ‘Shoey’ makes an appearance as a headpiece.

The final chapter looked at the current McLaren era and the audience surrounding it. One group played with the idea of young fans seeing drivers as heroes, using toy cars, childlike drawings and a cape-like silhouette, while used McLaren racing boots from previous eras were brought back for the finished look.

The way fans interact with Formula 1 now was one of the reasons McLaren wanted to do the project in the first place.

During the panel, F1 Presenter Ariana Bravo spoke about just how much the audience around the sport has changed.

“Formula 1 has seen a growth in its audience in a way that I don’t think any of us within the sport were expecting," she said. "It’s a much younger and a much more diverse audience now.

“With that comes a different way that people want to consume our sport. It’s not just about watching the cars go around on track anymore. It’s about everything that surrounds that as well.

“Yes, of course, they’re fans of the racing first and foremost, but they also want to tap into the culture. They want to tap into the lifestyle aspect of it. They don’t want to just tap into the drivers in race mode. They want to have this accessibility 24/7, and they want to be able to express their support for a team through fashion, through culture.”

McEwen told F1.com that Global F1 Fan data shows nearly half of fans consider fashion important to the way they express their fandom. That data helped inform the project, although McEwen says success cannot simply be measured in reach or engagement.

“We are obsessed by data, and the whole piece tonight was informed by data," she said. "The fact that our fans, and half of F1 fans broadly, actually say that fashion is important to them and it’s how they show their fandom.

“But everything that you saw today was very much about creativity and humanness coming through.

“In terms of measurement, I think it’s a blend. It’s not one or the other. Tonight we opened the doors to the McLaren Technology Centre to many in the media who had never been here before, probably seeing a different side of us and our sport.

“Hopefully that will reach many new fans who might have been thinking about Formula 1, might not know anything about Formula 1, but might be fashion lovers, and vice versa. I think it’s just about that crossover between popular culture and sport that we’re seeing so much of right now.”

That changing audience was visible off the runway too, with guests from across motorsport, fashion, music and sport inside the McLaren Technology Centre for the show.

McLaren team mates Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were joined by F1 ACADEMY drivers Ella Lloyd and Ella Stevens, as well as Freddie Hunt, son of James.

But also in attendance were models Mia Regan, Amechi Madu and Denola Gray, rapper Kojey Radical and Olympic medallist Amy Hunt.

McLaren are far from alone in embracing fashion, but McEwen is wary of suggesting any team can assume they have already worked out what this newer audience wants.

“I think in this game, you can never think you’re ahead of the curve, right?" she added. "There’s always someone just behind you waiting to catch up.

“I like to think that, as a team, we’ve really driven innovation in this space. Tonight again, I think we’ve shown another side of us. Showing up in a space where performance meets culture with that authenticity has been really important to us, and establishing a relationship with Central Saint Martins.”

For McEwen, giving creatives the freedom to interpret McLaren in their own way was also central to the project, and something she believes is just as important away from the track.

“We have to be as competitive off the grid as we are on it, and I think the point is, without creativity, we’re never going to appeal to new fans, we’re never going to have new ideas, and I think you’ve got to be really careful not to stifle that creativity.

“Tonight, you can see what can happen when you give people a little bit of inspiration, but then give them that scope to go and design and see where they want to go.

“I didn’t know quite what we were going to get tonight, and I’m just blown away and super excited.”

title: Why Williams' FW48 upgrade package in Baku is so crucial
excerpt:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix will be a huge weekend for the Williams team as they finally introduce the long-awaited major upgrade package for the FW48.

Up until now the 2026 season has been a painful one for drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon, especially in the light of the promise shown last year.

Delays forced the team to miss the Barcelona Shakedown, and when it finally took to the track the car proved to be significantly overweight, as well as having some inherent issues.

At an early stage, much like Aston Martin, the team took the decision to focus on a major package for the second half of the season, although in the case of Williams some new bits have been introduced along the way, such as a revised front wing for Silverstone. There has also been an ongoing programme of trimming weight.

However, the results tell their own story. In the early races the drivers managed to log five points finishes, with a best of P8 for Albon in the high attrition Monaco Grand Prix. However, since then the team have failed to score a single point, with the cars typically finishing in the P15, P16 and P17 range.

In part that’s down to an improved reliability record across the field since the early races, but it also reflects the fact that rivals have been improving while Williams have made little progress.

“I think what's been interesting this year is most of the midfield teams, they always bring one or two upgrades a year,” Albon noted after a difficult race in Madrid last weekend. “That's kind of how it's gone. This year, even the midfield teams are bringing three or four upgrades a year, and the size of upgrades are huge as well.

“So if you think of us in a normal year, Baku would have put us back in contention. But we have to be honest with ourselves, the speed of the development race this year is huge – and yeah, we've fallen back.”

In other words, when the Baku package was signed off several months ago the numbers looked promising in terms of the potential gains. However, as other midfield cars have improved, the goalposts have moved.

The FW48 will be faster, there’s little doubt – but it’s all relative, and there might not be the dramatic surge up the grid that may have originally seemed possible.

It is also likely to be the last roll of the dice for Williams in 2026, as the focus turns increasingly to next season and the FW50.

“We're finishing realistically 50 seconds behind the midfield at the minute in a race,” said Albon. “So we're losing a second a lap, more or less, in the race, and this has to be a pretty big upgrade to do it. Let's see.

“We know it's going to be a good step. Is it going to be the full step? I'm hopeful for it, but I don't think it will be. Unfortunately, we said it last year, but the focus is on next year as well. And we realise we're too far back at the moment to have a couple of upgrades for this year. We need to focus on next year.”

Last year Sainz qualified second and finished third in Azerbaijan, a reminder of just how competitive Williams were at some venues. Like Albon, the Spaniard is keeping his expectations in check.

“I think that upgrade is going to definitely help us to get ourselves closer to potentially fighting for some points,” he said at his home race. “But realistically speaking, that’s nowhere near where we wanted to be this year, nowhere near what we promised. So, it’s still not enough, and it’s still not where we want to be.

How Sainz's home race in Madrid unravelled

“It’s an upgrade that will help a bit the motivation of the team and just to look into the weekend with something to look forward to, maybe to potentially get a point or two when we were like we were at the beginning of the year.

“But it’s nowhere near where we want to be, and I think our biggest hope is putting all the eggs in next year’s basket.”

Sainz makes a good point about motivation. The Baku package might not allow the team to move into contention for Q3, but the important thing is that it brings the performance gains that were calculated months ago.

That would be a demonstration that the processes are working, and will also give the design team the confidence that they are going in the right direction with the FW50.

Baku is thus crucial for Team Principal James Vowles, the man tasked with taking Williams back to title contention, and who a few weeks ago convinced Albon and Sainz to commit for the future.

Vowles highlighted changes in processes and methodology and a wave of key recruits (such as Chief Optimisation and Planning Officer Piers Thynne) as reasons for the drivers to have faith that the team won’t make the same mistakes that they made ahead of 2026.

“You're making a thousand decisions in the winter,” Vowles noted at Zandvoort. “You don't need many of them to be wrong before you start putting yourself into the wrong path. And that'll be the difference between a few tenths, but a few tenths these days is the between winning a championship or not.

“You go to the level of what are the big building blocks you're putting in place? Which is a combination of people, which is different to what we had before. A combination of strength in the team that was different to what we had before.

“And for us, we had a lack last year at the beginning of '25 of simulation technology. That actually only came online in November last year. The car was already pretty much done by that point in time.

“So what we were doing was using educated guessing, and we got some of it wrong. If you look at our rear ride height, we developed at the wrong rear ride height, as did Aston, for that matter, and corrected it.

“That doesn't seem like a huge amount. But you're aerodynamically developing in completely the wrong space, and it's not driven by anything more than simulation telling you that's a good direction for whatever characteristic you're after, and it goes wrong.

“That error can still be made across any winter, because you're in a theoretical space against a maximal space.”

If it does what it’s supposed to do, the Baku package will be a sign that things are moving in the right direction at Grove.

However, Vowles makes no guarantees that there won’t be some missteps with the development of the 2027 car: “Not for a second am I going to promise anyone, because there's no championship team that would.

“What you're more trying to do is show that there's enough depth that didn't exist previously in the ways of working systems, tools, processes, and people that allow you to catch as many of those as possible.”

title: Inside the Italian dinner party staged on Monza's grid
excerpt:
The world of Formula 1 is passionate, high-energy and non-stop, so the opportunity to truly slow down and take it all in is one that shouldn’t be passed up. Barilla recognised the unique chance to do just that in a short moment of peace ahead of the Italian Grand Prix.

A fortunate group made up of drivers both past and present, team members, journalists and fans were invited to enjoy an exquisite three-course meal cooked by Michelin-starred chef Massimo Bottura, who admitted that the prospect of cooking pasta perfectly al dente for hundreds of people was a somewhat daunting task.

Before the time for that came, I ventured down the eerily quiet pit lane – usually a place punctuated by the noise of wheel guns and hubbub of mechanics – to the grid entrance, where Barilla representatives handed over a pass labelled ‘La Tavolata’ and a much-needed handheld fan.

We were well into the evening hours, but the tarmac insistently emitted the heat it had absorbed through the day, so I was more than grateful for the token. It was similarly branded with the event name – an Italian term for a large crowd sharing a meal at a single, shared table.

And that was exactly what filled the starting grid. I couldn’t help but take in the enormity of the long table, draped in a white cloth with accents of dark blue, while wine glasses sparkled in the last of the sun’s light. The grandstands were empty, but a Ferrari flag acted as a reminder of the action to come.

The chatter of this F1 microcosm grew louder as I headed towards the iconic five red lights, where small tables were surrounded by stalls offering bruschetta, cured meat, cheese, champagne and breadsticks, all covered by canopies in the same white and blue colourway.

A roaming band made up of four players flexed their talents with crowd-pleasers by The Beatles, visiting each huddle of attendees in turn and making it practically impossible to avoid smiling – even more so when they switched to irresistible Italian classics like Mambo Italiano and Sarà Perché Ti Amo.

From Ascari to Antonelli – Monza’s most magical home wins

After I consumed a borderline embarrassing number of hors d’oeuvres, we were directed to take our seats and inspect the menu. For someone who adores both F1 and food, this experience was my equivalent of a dog hearing the words ‘walk’ or ‘treat’.

Barilla pasta, pesto, dessert, Monza, starting grid… it was getting pretty hard to hide my excitement, and I was far from alone – everyone had a look in their eyes that conveyed an appreciative disbelief at the whole evening.

First up was Fusilloni Al Bronzo al Pesto, which the menu described as a “reinterpretation of traditional Ligurian pesto” with a pea cream and toasted breadcrumbs, creating a “testimony to extraordinary flavours”.

“I'm a little bit stressed because I'm thinking about 35 kilos of pasta that has to come out al dente at least – it's not easy and my hands are sweating,” Bottura conceded in his welcome speech. “I feel a little butterfly in my stomach, but okay, it’s part of the challenge so I'll do it.

“This is exactly the example of the classic Italian Tavolata. You know, we sit together, we share together. This is Italian cuisine and this is the reason because the Italian cuisine has been named UNESCO Heritage. It's not because Italian cuisine is one cuisine. There are 100,000 cuisines in Italy.

“It's their ritual of sitting around the table, sharing a meal in a refectory or in a three Michelin star restaurant. It's the same. Cooking is an act of love, that's it. And when you do it, you do it for your friends, for your family, or for the F1 family.”

He went on to outline the fresh, aromatic herbs that blended together to make the most vibrant green pesto I’ve ever seen, marking the first of two dishes to showcase Barilla pasta. The next was the main course – affectionately titled ‘Lap Two’ to tie in further with our location.

Barilla went above and beyond in their role as an F1 Official Partner by making a limited edition pasta called Gran Ruote. Inspired by the shape of wheels, its spokes are perfectly placed to capture all the sauce, which in this case was a delightfully simple cacio e pepe made from Parmigiano Reggiano and pepper.

Last up was the final lap of the meal: ‘L’essenza del Sole Siciliano’. Bottura described this creation as “a beautiful idea of the power of the sun, of the beauty of Italy”.

Michelin-starred chef Massimo Bottura reveals his F1 heroes

“For me, when I think about Italy and I think of the sun, I think Sicily,” he explained. “The whole dessert is like the power of Sicily with all the citrus and almonds and capers and coffee and the fruit of Sicily.”

It was a refreshing conclusion to a night in which I like to think I achieved the aim of La Tavolata – sharing conversations with those from all walks of F1 and coming together to bask in a community unlike any other. Paolo Barilla, a former racer himself, summarised that feeling well with a story from his childhood.

“In 1974 I was there [indicating a nearby grandstand],” he relayed to the crowd of diners. “I wanted to see Formula 1 from very close, but it was far. Two Ferraris were leading – Clay Regazzoni and Niki Lauda – and both of them retired.

“I was 13 years old. I was desperate. Disaster! My first Grand Prix, my heart beating for Ferrari and I see two Ferraris stop at the beginning of the pit lane. In 1975, Ferrari got first place with Clay Regazzoni and third place with Niki and they won the championship.

“And then I go to 1980, when I made the first lap with Formula Fiat Abarth here. Going there to the first chicane, I felt the immensity of this place, the history on my shoulders, and I was amazed by the emotion I felt. I would say that Monza, between the highs and lows, it's an emotional place.

“To have all of you here around the table where we want the people to get together, share the emotion, and then on Sunday they have to fight. The fight is a part of life, but the friendship around the table is very important.”

title: Football legend José Mourinho on his love for F1
excerpt:
Two worlds came together at last weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix when legendary football coach – and long-time F1 fan – José Mourinho paid a visit to the Madring circuit to follow the action.

Ahead of Sunday’s race, which took place just a stone’s throw away from Real Madrid’s training ground, F1.com grabbed a few words with the Portuguese tactician to discuss the Spanish capital’s all-new Grand Prix, his passion for racing, and how F1 compares (and differs) to football…

It’s Saturday night in Madrid and the streets are buzzing with Real fans who, after watching their team beat Inter Milan 2-1 in the Champions League mid-week, expect more of the same from a La Liga fixture against Rayo Vallecano.

Once inside the 83,000-capacity Bernabéu stadium, Mourinho and his group of star players waste no time in putting on a show – Los Blancos racing into a 3-0 lead by half-time with goals from the likes of Kylian Mbappé and Jude Bellingham. By the end of the game, a commanding 4-1 scoreline brings them level on points with rivals FC Barcelona at the top of the table.

Some 12 hours later, after a well-earned rest, Mourinho, Bellingham and other team members have swapped that hallowed turf for new ground in the form of the Madring – F1’s hybrid street/permanent circuit built around the IFEMA Exhibition Centre, and less than four kilometres from Madrid’s training pitches.

Mourinho is no stranger to the F1 paddock, having made several visits in previous seasons, including last year’s British Grand Prix, but there is something particularly meaningful for him this time around.

“I’ve enjoyed it [F1] for a while, and I’ve been to a few races, but of course this is the first one [at the Madring],” Mourinho tells F1.com.

“Because I work just around the corner, every day that I was coming to work or leaving work, I was following it, the building [process], and the more we were approaching this day, [there was] more emotion for everybody.”

Given that Mourinho has gone from the football field to the F1 grid on multiple occasions, it begs an obvious question: what do the two sports have in common, and how are they different?

For the 63-year-old, who has also managed Manchester United, Inter Milan, Chelsea and Roma, among other clubs, there is a standout common theme – as well as an area in which he feels football can learn from F1.

“You know, it’s huge pressure for both,” he says thoughtfully. “When you have sports at the highest level, we are always speaking about huge pressure.

“But I feel that they [F1] are one step ahead of us in terms of the way they approach the big moments. [In football] we close each other [off], I believe, too much, also because of tradition.

“These guys [the drivers], [there’s] huge pressure, but before that [time in the car], they are together, they meet people, they do a little bit of PR, they do a little bit of media.

“I think we have to learn with them, the way they can be relaxed, and half an hour later they can be in the car fighting for their lives, because they take risks.”

Since his first managerial stint with Portuguese club Benfica back in 2000, Mourinho has racked up more than 25 major trophies – the UEFA Champions League, the UEFA Cup/Europa League, the Premier League, the FA Cup, other national titles and plenty more, along with a host of individual accolades.

However, what about the hypothetical challenge of leaving football behind and becoming an F1 team boss?

“I have no idea!” Mourinho responds, with his eyes widening at the prospect. “I just have to learn. I learn with [F1 President and CEO] Stefano Domenicali; I ask him lots of questions. I tried to learn with all of them [the people I meet], and I like very much to come [to watch F1].

“It was not possible [on Saturday], because I had a match day, but I like to come for the Qualifyings, I like to come for the training sessions [Free Practices], because then clearly you can be closer, and you can interact more.

“Today is their day, and it’s the day I like to respect their privacy.”

Nonetheless, Mourinho has met and struck up friendships with many F1 drivers and personalities since experiencing the sport for the first time – his tour of the Madring on Sunday still featuring various catch-ups and motorhome visits.

That included conversations with the aforementioned Domenicali, and four-time World Champion Max Verstappen, who was presented with his pole position award by Mourinho at Silverstone in 2025.

“I know almost all of them, and everybody [has been] so nice to me over so many years,” Mourinho continues. “Now we’re coming to some new people, to some new generations, but I always had great respect from them.

“Because, as a family, we are so close to Stefano, it is of course a great way to be invited – we invited ourselves! – and to have always the reception that we have.”

Mourinho’s latest visit might have been a fleeting one, but judging by his comments above, there is no doubt that one of football’s most iconic figures will be back for more in the future.

title: Mekies offers update on Hadjar's injury recovery
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has missed the three races since the summer break ended, sitting out Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid as he recovers from an injury sustained in training. The Frenchman hurt his wrist in the three-week break, and has been on the sidelines ever since.

In his absence, Liam Lawson has stepped up into the vacant Red Bull seat, with Yuki Tsunoda filling Lawson’s cockpit at Racing Bulls.

Those two have done an admirable job in difficult circumstances, but they face a wait to see just who will be where for the next Grand Prix in Azerbaijan.

Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies clarified the situation in the wake of the Spanish Grand Prix, confirming that there had been no additional setbacks for Hadjar, and that his recovery was taking as long as expected.

“Isack is good... There is nothing wrong with Isack's recovery. I think we have learned that it's fundamentally normal time for the sort of injuries he has,” Mekies said.

“So, we will continue with the same approach than what we had, we will evaluate the situations in a weeks’ time, we have a full week, with more than a full week to evaluate the situation to see how he feels.

“And then to put him on the simulator, to expose him to real-life constraints… If he feels close to 100%, we go for it. If he feels the recovery is not completed, we will stick [with] our approach to put his recovery first.

“What we don't want to do is by having an early return, compromise his long-term capacity to come back to 100%.”

Hadjar has made a strong start to his time with Red Bull, with eight top-10 finishes, including a podium in Monaco. He has also managed to out-qualify Max Verstappen three times.

This injury setback is far from ideal, with the Frenchman having missed out not just on points, but on learning more about the RB22 as everyone continues to get to grips with the new generation of cars.

He has still attended races and thus will have been looking at the data, but that is not the same as driving and understanding exactly where the latest upgrades are taking the car.

In his absence, Verstappen has taken two podiums to show what the car is capable of, while Lawson has finished in the points twice from his three drives with the team.

Another driver in recent memory to come back from a wrist injury was Lance Stroll, who had a bicycle accident prior to the start of the season in 2023. He missed testing but drove in the opening race and scored points despite having a broken wrist and toe.

Daniel Ricciardo was out considerably longer than Stroll when he broke a bone in his hand in 2023 after crashing in practice at Zandvoort. The Australian wound up missing five Grands Prix – with Lawson being his replacement at the time.

It seems that Red Bull are happy to leave it late to make a call on whether Hadjar will return to the cockpit for the upcoming triple header, or whether he will remain on the sidelines for the time being.

title: 'Bit of a shock to the system' leading Cadillac – Budkowski
excerpt:
Marcin Budkowski admits that returning to Formula 1 has been "a bit of a shock to the system", having been put in charge of the Cadillac team.

The Pole has been with the American team for nearly a month, having replaced Graeme Lowdon as Team Principal just before the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August.

Budkowski is no stranger to F1, having worked with multiple championship-winning Formula 1 teams across sporting and technical divisions and within senior leadership teams, including Prost, McLaren, Alpine and the FIA.

Having left the sport in 2022, Budkowski found himself in a new role with media organisations Eleven Sports Poland and Viaplay, before the call from Cadillac.

Ahead of last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, Budkowski admitted that the return to a prominent role in the sport had been a bit of a shock.

"What hits you first is the pace of F1, which I knew well but a few years out of the sport and it's a bit of a shock to the system because it's incredibly fast-paced, technical and hard-working, especially when you start in a new team and new project," said Budkowski during Friday's teams' press conference.

"The other thing is the first time I sat again on the pit wall in FP1 in Zandvoort and I had 12 channels blasting in my ears. It took me a little bit of time for my brain to get used to it.

"But the reality is, if you bring it back to the essentials and basics, it's about people, it's about building the team. It's about putting the right people in the right positions, getting everybody to work together and in terms of leadership, give them a vision and align everybody in that direction. That hasn't changed."

Cadillac have endured a difficult maiden season in F1 so far, remaining the only team on the grid yet to score a point, with Valtteri Bottas' P13 in the Chinese Grand Prix the team's best result to date.

Despite the lack of pace and reliability so far, Budkowski has been encouraged by what he has seen, despite having been at the helm for only three races.

"I've seen a lot of good things in the team, and it's pretty impressive given the time they had to build the team and conditions with the entry and everything.

"A lot of good things, there's no legacy compared to some other teams. There's a lot of open-minded, constructive discussions going on but there's also a number of shortcuts that are being taken, which is inevitable when you build a new team in such a time.

"It's about working in some areas that need more attention. In the short-term, reliability. We've seen we've struggled with that in some areas and just getting the operational excellence to the next level, which is not the level of a top team as of today, but that's understandable.

"Longer term, there's some clearer priorities emerging for what we need to do and better, mostly to improve our performance and our pace."

title: Liam Lawson offers response to Max Verstappen 'numb' F1 car claim
excerpt:
Liam Lawson says he can understand where Max Verstappen is coming from with his view that he and Yuki Tsunoda have adjusted quickly to their new F1 cars, but not fully.

Lawson has been temporarily promoted to Red Bull since the Dutch GP as Isack Hadjar continues his recovery from a broken wrist sustained during the summer break, with Tsunoda drafted in to replace the New Zealander in turn.

Lawson has scored a sixth, a seventh, and a 14th from his three races, whilst Tsunoda picked up a point in the Italian GP at Monza in just his second race in the new generation of car, which features high level of energy management owing to the design of the new power units.

Because of this, senior Red Bull driver Verstappen has explained that he feels the cars are "numb to driver inputs" and that the "immediate competitive" performances were related to the 2026 machines being easier to drive as drivers were placed "in a choke-hold" and that they were "held back" from performing at their best.

Verstappen did concede that "you still have to do a good lap and commit" as Lawson explained he could understand where his team leader was coming from, but did not necessarily agree.

"I don't know, I mean, it is something that the cars in general, they're not simpler because they're actually quite complicated in the way that you to [drive], the way the energy is," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365, when asked if he agreed with Verstappen's assessment.

"I can understand it as there are things that are maybe less in our control in the way the energy is [managed], but at the same time, it is myself and Yuki who have jumped in these cars.

"We're the only ones that know what it's like to try and get up to speed in the new car, so it is definitely not a simple thing.

"You could say, yes, maybe getting up to speed and the gaps between the teams are a bit bigger this year, and they haven't been that big recently; it's been pretty tight, so you could look at it like that and say: 'Okay, maybe they're a little bit simpler to get up to speed.

"But there are many things that I have personally in my own [Racing Bulls] car that I've got used to over the last year and a half that I've liked that I can't just go and apply in a car like this."

The article continues below.

Lawson explains Red Bull vs Racing Bulls difference

Lawson then went on to explain how some creature comforts in his Racing Bulls machine were not present in the Red Bull cockpit he's currently occupying.

"There are things that haven't been very comfortable with in the last few races that I've been trying to almost drive around, and those are things that are not just simple on paper that you would that you would see," he continued.

"But just a personal driver thing: everybody has things in their own car that they're comfortable with.

"So I think as much as maybe all the cars are okay to jump in and drive, and maybe they are reasonably simple to get up to speed, it's that kind of stuff that I've been trying to get my head around in the last couple of weeks that are different from my car."

title: Former F1 race director Michael Masi speaks out as new role confirmed
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 race director Michael Masi has been appointed as the new head of sporting at SRO Motorsports Australia, the organisation responsible for running GT World Challenge Australia as part of its Shannons SpeedSeries network.

The appointment is described as effective immediately, though Masi will undergo an official handover period before assuming the role on a full-time basis from 2027.

As part of that transition, he will attend the final two rounds of the 2026 season in Sydney and Adelaide.

Masi held the position of F1 race director between 2019 and 2021, a tenure that ended in the wake of the infamous Abu Dhabi Grand Prix finale.

In his new capacity, Masi will be responsible for the organisation's rules and regulations, oversight of race officials including the stewards, and aligning SRO Motorsports Australia with the broader SRO Global processes and best practices.

Reacting to the news, Masi expressed enthusiasm for the challenge ahead: "This is an extremely exciting opportunity to be part of the next chapter for SRO Motorsports Australia, and I'm looking forward to continuing the great work that has already been done by the team and particularly Abi [Hay]."

"GT racing in Australia has been on a steady rise, and I'm confident there is plenty of opportunity to continue building on the strong foundations that have already been established."

"I'm looking forward to working with everyone involved and hopefully implementing some positive initiatives that can further develop the sport and deliver benefits for competitors, teams and all of our stakeholders."

SRO Motorsports Australia CEO Ben McMellan was equally positive about bringing Masi on board: "We are delighted to have someone of Michael's stature joining SRO Motorsports Australia for the remainder of the 2026 season and beyond."

"Michael brings an enormous amount of experience from decades spent at the top positions of motorsport, and we're confident his knowledge and expertise will help take GT racing in Australia to the next level."

title: Colton Herta names 'chaotic' F1 experience he actually enjoys
excerpt:
Colton Herta has explained how he actually "enjoys" the "hectic" experience of changing between F1 and F2 machinery when he is on Cadillac duty.

The American racer has taken the MAC-26 out for three FP1 sessions thus far in 2026 as he completes a full season in FIA F2, and has driven in Barcelona, Hungary, and Italy.

His fourth and final FP1 outing of the season has yet to be confirmed, but it is unlikely to clash again with F1, meaning he will not have to dovetail running both machines on a Friday morning.

In his last outing in Italy, Herta crashed in F2 practice before quickly getting adjusted to take over Sergio Perez's car.

However, the former IndyCar star has detailed how he actually enjoys the experience of chopping and changing between the cars.

"It's very enjoyable. Actually, it's very hectic," Herta began to media, including RacingNews365.

"You don't have time to sit down and think about anything other than what you're doing next.

"You're constantly just going from meeting to meeting to meeting and car to car to car. So I find it very enjoyable.

"I like how chaotic and hectic it is, and how much time you get in the cars.

"So it definitely is tough to jump between them, but I enjoy the process of it."

The article continues below.

Herta's progression in F1

As for his getting up to speed in grand prix machinery, Herta felt that as he gains more experience, he is learning and "seeing improvements."

"I think it's just about getting comfortable and then understanding what the drivers think the main problems of the car are, and so then I can kind of expect a bit more and try to close down on that learning period," he added.

"Every time I've got in the car, it's been really nice, and you know the transition of coming up to speed.

"I think all it is is just time needed to be able to maximise it completely. But every time I'm seeing improvements, so it's positive."

title: Sebastian Vettel weighs in on major F1 concern
excerpt:
Sebastian Vettel has responded to the criticism that has been directed towards the new cars introduced this year.

F1 underwent a major regulations change for the 2026 campaign, with brand-new aerodynamic and power unit rules coming into play.

The latter element has drawn disapproval from several of the current drivers, who feel that overtaking relies more on the push of a button rather than utilising their skills.

Vettel was speaking in Monza earlier this month after jumping out from behind the wheel of Michael Schumacher's 2002 Ferrari, and insisted there is still plenty to get excited about in F1 today.

“It is exciting, racing is exciting,” Vettel told media including RacingNews365.

“I know what you mean and I know what the question is, and I think that’s why it’s so exciting, - there’s so much more to unpack when you look at Formula 1.

“Of course, from a driver’s point of view, ‘I want to drive the best car and I want to win races.’

“But then, what is the best car? The car of 2002 has been a state-of-the-art car at that time and a pioneer, and represents so much for what Formula 1 stands for.

“The cars today do the same, and I think it’s about performance, precision, discipline, hard work - but also responsibility and taking that forward. So also caring about the future, which these cars are trying to do.”

[Article continues below]

Vettel admits he 'doesn't agree' with all elements of current rules

The FIA has already confirmed that modifications will be made to the power units over the next couple of years in a bid to improve the experience for the driver.

While Vettel admitted he is also not fond of the engines, he insisted the sport remains in a healthy position.

“I’m probably not agreeing on everything that we currently have in the regulations, from a driving point of view,” he said.

“But looking forward, that’s where there’s a huge chance to take people on board, and maybe also through a moment like today, remind them what the sport was, what the sport is, and what the sport should be and can be in the future, and to do it responsibly.

“One doesn’t have to exclude the other. We need to find practices with everything that we are able to combine things that we love.”

title: Sergio Perez shares Cadillac Baku plan as 'painful' prediction made
excerpt:
Sergio Perez is hopeful Cadillac will finally deploy the new upgraded Ferrari engine for the first time at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Ferrari introduced its first ADUO-assisted upgrade at the Italian Grand Prix with both works drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc taking the new unit, as did Oliver Bearman at other Ferrari customer Haas.

Esteban Ocon and both Cadillac drivers have not yet taken the upgraded unit, which aims to eradicate some of the straight-line speed deficit the unit has compared to the Mercedes HPP design.

Cadillac remains without a point 14 races into its debut season, with the best result being 13th for Valtteri Bottas in China, with Perez's own best being 14th in Barcelona and at Silverstone, although he did finish 10th in Monaco for one point before being stripped due to post-race penalty.

As the team looks to progress continually, Perez feels that deciding to take the available upgrade will be key.

"Baku is one of those races where you just have to put everything together and see what happens," Perez told media, including RacingNews365.

"I really hope that we are able to put the new engine in the car and make a bit of a step because we really need a little bit more.

"It is the plan at the moment.

"I think it is very clear what we're lacking: load and [too much] drag. But I was with the engineers, and there seems to be a very, very strong progress and a very strong direction going forward.

"So I'm really optimistic for what will come, and it will probably be a very painful end of the season as it's been in the first half, but that was expected, so I am pleased with how things are going."

Bottas echoes Perez

Bottas was unsure about whether both cars would take the engine upgrade, as he detailed where the MAC-26 was not "robust enough."

"We know we need to improve. The car is still not robust enough, and we need to make it a lot faster," he said.

"The [tyre] degradation [in the Spanish GP] highlights how much load we are lacking and we're sliding way more than the competition.

"I think in the beginning we can be there, but then as the race progresses, the deg gets worse, but actually, for the next event, I'm more hopeful that we can be there.

"In Baku, the only high-speed corners are to flat out, and so otherwise it's slow and medium speed corners."

title: Kimi Antonelli handed praise from major rival: 'An asset for F1'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has enjoyed a highly successful 2026 F1 season thus far and is closing in on a maiden title with Mercedes.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has hailed the impact Kimi Antonelli has had this year, stating he is an “asset for F1”.

Antonelli joined the F1 grid last year as a rookie driver but often struggled for form alongside his more experienced team-mate George Russell.

However, the Italian has taken a notable step forward this year with eight grands prix wins, leaving him with a sizeable lead in the drivers' championship.

With an 81-point advantage, Antonelli is seen as the favourite for the title as the campaign approaches its final third.

When asked if he has any advice for Antonelli, Stella told media including RacingNews365: “I would give him the wrong advice because we are chasing him!

“I care about Andrea Kimi, first of all, because he’s an asset for F1. He’s doing so well.

“Deservedly, he’s leading the drivers’ championship and, honestly, every time I hear from him, I see him, his stance, to me it looks like he’s growing day by day.

“So, he knows very well what to do. I’m sure he will keep this attitude, this speed, this consistency that he has expressed so far in the championship, and it will be a very difficult one to chase.”

Antonelli 'taking fans away from Ferrari'

Despite having a rich history with F1, Italy has been starved of F1 success of late, with Ferrari enduring a title drought that stretches back to 2008.

Alpine boss Flavio Briatore, who, like Stella, is Italian, highlighted that Antonelli has quickly established himself as one of the country's most recognisable sportsmen.

“In this moment in Italy you have two big names – [Janick] Sinner and Kimi,” he said.

“I think Kimi takes away the fans from Ferrari as well, little by little, because really it’s incredible what he is performing this year.

“He’s performing incredibly. No mistakes, very strong, very clear and still very, very young.

“And like Stella said, it’s good for F1 and it’s very good for Italy as well, because to have the potential champion like Kimi is good for the sport, it’s good for the country.

“And we are lucky we have two super guys, Sinner and Kimi.”

title: Max Verstappen left furious after multiple George Russell clashes - Throwback
excerpt:
Things got heated between Max Verstappen and George Russell during the 2023 Azerbaijan sprint race.

As the 2026 edition of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix inches closer, RacingNews365 has looked back on one of the most dramatic moments from the country's 10-year association with F1.

In 2023, Baku saw the first sprint format of the year, and it resulted in fireworks between Max Verstappen and George Russell.

It happened right at the start of the race - Russell dived to the inside in an attempt to outmanoeuvre Max Verstappen for third place. The two drove side by side through Turn 1, Turn 2, and Turn 3.

In Turn 2, however, Russell’s Mercedes, suffering from understeer, slid into the left side of the Red Bull, causing significant damage.

The sidepod and floor of Verstappen’s RB19 were damaged, with a visible hole in the bodywork.

As they entered Turn 3, Verstappen was then pushed wide and into the wall. The Dutchman lightly grazed the barrier and had to relinquish third place to Russell for good.

No investigation followed: race control and the FIA stewards classified the incident as a racing incident, with no further investigation or penalty for either driver.

[Article continues below]

Heated exchange after the race

Despite the damage to his car, Verstappen fought his way back to P3 in the sprint race, behind winner Sergio Perez and Charles Leclerc.

He passed Russell at the restart on lap 6, after which a sarcastic radio message followed. Gianpiero Lambiase said, “Lovely job, Max. Without contact, as well. Nicely done.”

Verstappen replied: “Yeah, I know how to do that, *****.”

After the sprint race, Verstappen sought out Russell in parc fermé to confront him about his move.

Russell, however, didn’t think he’d done anything wrong, stating: “I had no grip. I just locked up.”

Verstappen stated: “We all have no grip. We all need to leave a little bit of space.”

As Russell walked away and told Verstappen to check the onboard footage, Verstappen called after him: “Then, next time expect the same. Dickhead.”

A day later, in the main race, the battle between the two didn’t materialise: Verstappen finished second behind teammate Preez, while Russell crossed the finish line in eighth place, though he did set the fastest lap and earned an extra point.

title: Lando Norris names 'inevitable choice' as major team decision made
excerpt:
Lando Norris has described how he settled on the "inevitable choice" of Rene Rosin to lead his new LN4 Fusion junior racing team.

It was announced earlier this month that the 2025 F1 champion was to set up his own junior racing squad to initially compete in the Italian F4 Championship, FRECA and Formula 3.

The group has also acquired assets of AIX Racing, including its FIA F3 entry, and has lodged an application to join the FIA F2 grid.

The team principal of the squad will be Frenchman Rene Rosin, who, at the helm of the Prema squad creating a junior racing powerhouse before stepping down at the start of 2026 from the team his family founded.

Rosin has guided the likes of Charles Leclerc, Oscar Piastri, Mick Schumacher, Kimi Antonelli, and Oliver Bearman into F1 through his work at Prema, with Norris believing he was the obvious choice to lead his new team.

"A lot of the guys are people I've known for a long time, and I've known Rene for many years," Norris told media, including RacingNews365.

"Since I started to go into single-seaters, I've raced against Prema since F4 so back in 2015, and I know him personally reasonably well, and so do my team around me.

"We wanted to put together a group which is experienced and knows how to lead a team, and not just create one good team, whether that's in F2 or F3, but be able to put together a project and something long-term and know how to put people together.

"Over the last seven years, I've been able to experience what makes a good leader, a good team, and a lot of it starts with the person at the very top, and he is that person.

"He is a guy who loves what he does, which is winning and creating a successful team and bringing people together to maximise things, so he was the inevitable choice at the end of the day.

"I don't know if he was out of a job beforehand, but at the same time, he was available, and he was the guy we wanted, and he was the guy who was available."

The article continues below.

Rosin's impressive record

Under Rosin's guidance, especially in the mid-2010s and early 2020s, Prema was often regarded as the powerhouse team in the largely spec-junior racing categories.

The likes of Le Mans winner and WEC champion Kamui Kobayashi, Indy 500 winner Felix Rosenqvist and F1 race winners Esteban Ocon, Pierre Gasly, Leclerc, Piastri, and Antonelli passed through the team, with other F1 stars including Lance Stroll, Mick Schumacher, Zhou Guanyu and Bearman all driving for the squad.

Between 2016 and 2021, Prema won four of the six GP2/FIA F2 titles, with Gasly, Leclerc, Schumacher and Piastri all claiming the highest prize in junior motorsport.

For good measure, Prema also won FIA F3 in three successive years, with Robert Shwartzman, Piastri, and Dennis Hauger between 2019 and 2021.

title: Red Bull provide response to FIA president's plan to aid Honda
excerpt:
Red Bull boss Laurent Mekies has explained that the team is happy to "sit down" and discuss the future of the ADUO regulations following FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's plan to aid Honda to keep Fernando Alonso in F1.

Given Honda's struggles in the first-year of the new generation of power units and Alonso's wavering over whether he should stay in grand prix racing or call time at the end of his 23rd season, Ben Sulayem has proposed aiding Honda with further rules concessions to bring it into line with the other power unit manufacturers.

This would likely be done through the Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities mechanism, which permits those power units down on performance to the benchmark in terms of ICE power, which is currently Red Bull, extra upgrades.

The 2026 power unit design specs were homologated earlier this year, but to allow manufacturers to catch-up to the leading unit, ADUO was created, with Audi and Ferrari among those to have already delivered their first allotted upgrade.

Under the rules, Honda would be entitled to the same two upgrades in 2026 and in 2027 as Audi, and Ferrari, but Ben Sulayem is keen to go further to keep Alonso in F1, with the two-time champion fiercely critical of the direction the championship has gone in.

Red Bull was surprised that its in-house RBPT power unit was judged the best under ADUO, with Mekies explaining that the team would play its part in holding discussing around the regulations.

"I think as much as we cannot agree all the time, I think as a sport, we try to keep a fairly open look at the regulations," Mekies told media, including RacingNews365, when asked about Ben Sulayem's comments.

"You may recall that there was actually a change in the ADUO regulations earlier this year, precisely in order to help those who were much behind compared to what was initially voted on.

"So all the teams voted in favour of that for the benefit of the sport.

"If there is a situation that needs fixing or needs to be supported, we normally find solutions.

"I guess, more to your question, we will at some stage sit down and discuss the future of the ADUO regulations.

"The shortfalls, we know some of them, and I'm sure there'll be choices to address them."

The article continues below.

What did Ben Sulayem actually say?

At a recent business forum meeting in Madrid ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix, the FIA chief explained that it was "not acceptable" for Alonso to be in such uncompetitive machinery, and that a plan was in place to aid Honda.

"We did something earlier in May, legally, for the team, towards the engine, to go and improve," Ben Sulayem said.

"Then I said to him [Alonso], 'I’m not going to tell you what we are going to do. Please tell me what you want because you are the driver - tell me what you want us to do to improve these results.'

"Suddenly, you see everything change, and then I get a call, and then I had a meeting yesterday. We are here also to support."

title: Charles Leclerc wagers Mercedes bet after 'vicious circle' observation
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has spoken of the "vicious circle" Ferrari has found itself in with a lack of power from its F1 engine, as he wagered a bet on Mercedes.

The Scuderia has been running with an engine deficit all season to Mercedes, but has emerged as its closest rival in the championship as engineers at Maranello attempt to solve the problems.

The first of these is that the Ferrari turbo was designed to be small, as to eliminate turbo lag and provide excellent power at low speeds and in traction zones on throttle application.

The drawback is that the power unit is unable to produce top-end straight-line speed to match Mercedes, with Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton consistent in their observations that the Mercedes-powered cars seem to pull away at the end of long straights.

To counter this, Ferrari did bring an ADUO-boosted engine to the Italian Grand Prix, but Leclerc has spoken of the built-in advantages Mercedes seems to have.

"Honestly, it is kind of a vicious circle," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"I mean, as soon as you have a lot more power, then you are deploying later out of the corners, because the power unit is giving you more power out of the corners.

"So you are deploying later, and so you are cutting later.

"So I would bet on their ICE power being quite significantly more."

The article continues below.

Leclerc hopeful over engine

As for Leclerc's ADUO-boosted engine following his big Monza crash, the Monegasque is hopeful that the power unit avoided critical damage and can be used again.

However, if it is not, he will be forced into taking an engine penalty before the end of the season in order to introduce the new parts to his pool once again.

title: Kimi Antonelli shares Valentino Rossi dream for own F1 career
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has explained how he hopes to emulate Valentino Rossi's support among fans long after his career has ended.

Rossi, a seven-time premier-class MotoGP champion, last competed on two wheels in 2021, bringing down the curtain on a glittering career that made him one of the most famous competitors in all of motorsport.

He remains a popular figure, with fans often still seen in his merchandise at races, with his iconic #46 race number even half a decade on from his retirement.

At the other end of the spectrum, Antonelli is Italy's most successful F1 driver since 1953 and is in just his second season of grand prix racing, but is closing in on becoming the youngest-ever world champion, at just 20 years old.

Should he go on to shatter Sebastian Vettel's record from 2010, Antonelli would become the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953, and has spoken of his admiration for the public connection between Rossi and his fans, something the Mercedes driver hopes he can one day replicate.

"Very often, the races, he won them even before going down on the track," Antonelli told Automoto Italy of 89-time premier class winner, Rossi.

"He was very strong mentally. It would be nice to be able to experience this feeling. As an athlete, then, Vale was very complete, very fast, very strong in the race, especially on weekends that seemed uphill, when he started backwards and managed to recover.

"And he managed to attract a huge audience. Even today you can see people wearing his merchandise at MotoGP races even if he doesn't race anymore.

"It would be wonderful to recreate the same effect in F1: the esteem, the support, the cheering. It's a very beautiful thing."

The article continues below.

Not just Rossi

Antonelli is also firm friends with current MotoGP star Marco Bezzecchi and other stars of Italian sport, including long-jumper Mattia Furlani, who won gold at the 2025 World Championships, and current world number one Men's tennis player, the five-time grand slam winner, Jannik Sinner.

Given the high-pressure environment all compete in, Antonelli then spoke of the positives of having such friends in elite sport.

"It's wonderful to have sports friends who compete at the highest levels, who understand what it means to manage pressure, the moments before a race, when you need to have your own space," Antonelli said.

"I'm also very close to Mattia Furlani, whom I met in Monza. It's nice to have these kinds of bonds, because they give you additional motivation to do even better.

"I'm glad to see them win, and I'd like to do the same, if not better. Even if doing better than Sinner is difficult.

"I consider Bezzecchi one of my best friends. We support each other, and when I can, I go to his races. When we are at home, we both go out for dinner together, and our groups of friends have joined. What he does is really crazy."

title: Fernando Alonso highlights 'biggest legacy' in F1 career reflection
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has a long association with F1, and sits as the most experienced driver in the sport's history.

Fernando Alonso has highlighted what he believes is his biggest “legacy” to F1 following a quarter of a century in the sport.

Having made his debut in 2001, Alonso has gone on to start a record-setting 439 grands prix - with the latest being a new event in his home country of Spain.

A fresh track was built in Madrid, with the event signing a 10-year deal with F1 to take over as host of the Spanish Grand Prix.

Throughout his career, Alonso has picked up two championships and 32 grand prix wins, but the 45-year-old insisted he feels more pride over the impact he has had in his home country.

“I feel honoured,” Alonso told media including RacingNews365.

“My debut in 2001, my family was watching my races on RTL, the German channel, because it was not broadcast in Spain.

“So that tells you how small F1 was 20 years ago and how much things have changed, and the passion for many drivers in Spain to become part of F1.

“And not only behind the wheel. I think there are maybe five, seven, 10% of the mechanics, engineers in F1 are now Spanish. So that’s probably another thing that we changed in Spain, the wish to be part of F1 in different roles.

“That’s the biggest, one of the most proud things that I feel.”

[Article continues below]

Driver

Alonso 'more proud' of Spanish impact than F1 career

Alonso's highs of title-winning campaigns came early in his career, with his last championship campaign being 20 years ago, while he has not won a grand prix in 13 years.

While he feels “lucky” to have experienced such success, Alonso gave special attention to his impact outside his personal results.

“Winning races or winning championships if you have the car and you are in the right place, right moment, the 20 drivers here, they can have that opportunity,” he said.

“I was very lucky to experience that.

“But I think the biggest legacy for me and my career is the change in Spain, for F1 and everything from karting, single-seaters, different Spanish teams racing in single-seaters, even to an extent in rally and other categories, my museum in Spain and all the visits that we have there.

“I don’t know, there are many things outside the car that maybe make me more proud of my career than the results itself.”

title: Toto Wolff confirms 'unlock' needed to baffling George Russell mystery
excerpt:
It is a mystery as to why George Russell has struggled this season in comparison to Kimi Antonelli.

Toto Wolff has conceded Mercedes still does not fully understand why George Russell is adrift of Kimi Antonelli's pace this season, insisting the team must "analyse" the issue rather than accept it as a simple driving-style mismatch.

Following a strong start to the season with victory in the Australian Grand Prix, Russell has taken the chequered flag on only one other occasion. In contrast, Antonelli has scored eight wins, one more than the British driver has achieved in his F1 career.

It has allowed Antonelli to open up an 81-point cushion over Russell, with the likelihood there are only eight grands prix remaining. It is expected a race in Europe will replace the final two in Qatar and Abu Dhabi to conclude the campaign.

Speaking on the pace gap between his drivers, Wolff said he remains puzzled by Russell's inconsistency, as occurred in Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring.

"You can see the pace he had towards the end when he was catching [Charles] Leclerc, when he was fastest out on track," said Wolff, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"After the tyre change, the pace was there. I just don't know where it is. We have to analyse because clearly it's in him, it's in the car, and we have to unlock it."

[Article continues below]

Driver

George Russell

British

63

A car built for a different style

Russell himself has pointed to a fundamental clash between his driving technique and this year's cars following the regulations change, which reward high-rotation corner entry and active weight transfer over the smoother, geometric inputs he favours.

He has, however, already conceded the title fight is beyond his control this year, stating that, "right now, Kimi deserves to be leading; right now, he deserves to be the champion this season."

Wolff, for his part, insists the imbalance between his drivers is nothing new to his style of management.

"I've had it for 15 years or so, that one part of the garage is happy, the other one not," he said. "It's just part of the sport, part of the job.

"The only thing I can try is to be transparent and honest about things. We talk about each and every scenario, and give the biggest support we can to both drivers, no matter what.

"Sometimes it's about putting an arm around a driver, sometimes putting a little bit more pressure, so that's what I need to do, and then I feel a little bit better about it."
